cards.front: A histogram is used for grouped [ ___ ] data.
cards.back: A histogram is used for grouped continuous data.

options.explanation: Histograms represent grouped continuous data because measurements can take any value within each class interval, and the bars cover adjoining numerical ranges.
Discrete data consists of separate, countable values and is usually represented using a bar chart. The correct term is continuous because histogram classes cover uninterrupted ranges.
Categorical data is divided into named groups rather than numerical intervals and is normally shown on a bar chart. Histograms are used for grouped continuous data.
Ungrouped data lists individual observations rather than organising them into class intervals. A histogram is specifically used to represent grouped continuous data.

cards.front: In a bar chart, [ ___ ] shows frequency; in a histogram, [ ___ ] shows frequency.
cards.back: In a bar chart, height shows frequency; in a histogram, area shows frequency.

options.text: In a bar chart, height shows frequency; in a histogram, area shows frequency.
options.explanation: Bar-chart frequencies are read directly from bar heights. In a histogram, frequency is proportional to bar area because class intervals can have different widths.

options.text: In a bar chart, area shows frequency; in a histogram, height shows frequency.
options.explanation: This reverses the two conventions. Height represents frequency in a bar chart, whereas area represents frequency in a histogram because histogram class widths may vary.

options.text: In a bar chart, width shows frequency; in a histogram, area shows frequency.
options.explanation: Bar width does not encode frequency in a bar chart; the height does. Histogram frequency is represented by area, calculated from class width and frequency density.

options.text: In a bar chart, height shows frequency; in a histogram, width shows frequency.
options.explanation: Histogram width represents the class width, not the frequency. Frequency is represented by the bar’s area, while bar-chart frequency is represented by height.

cards.front: In a histogram, bar width is [ ___ ] and bar height is [ ___ ].
cards.back: In a histogram, bar width is class width and bar height is frequency density.

options.text: In a histogram, bar width is class width and bar height is frequency density.
options.explanation: Each bar spans its class interval, so its width is the class width. Its height is frequency density, ensuring that the bar’s area represents frequency.

options.text: In a histogram, bar width is class width and bar height is frequency.
options.explanation: The width is correctly identified, but histogram height is frequency density, not frequency. Multiplying frequency density by class width gives the frequency represented by the area.

options.text: In a histogram, bar width is frequency density and bar height is class width.
options.explanation: This swaps the two quantities. Bar width represents class width along the horizontal axis, while bar height represents frequency density on the vertical axis.

options.text: In a histogram, bar width is class midpoint and bar height is cumulative frequency.
options.explanation: A class midpoint is a single central value, not a bar width, and cumulative frequency belongs to cumulative frequency graphs. The required quantities are class width and frequency density.

cards.front: The interval $0 \le t < 5$ includes 0 but not [ ___ ].
cards.back: The interval $0 \le t < 5$ includes 0 but not 5.

options.explanation: The strict inequality $t < 5$ excludes the upper endpoint 5, while the inequality $0 \le t$ includes the lower endpoint 0.
The symbol $\le$ means 0 is included in the interval. The excluded endpoint is 5 because the strict inequality $t < 5$ does not include equality.
Values below 5, including 4, are contained in the interval. The upper endpoint 5 is excluded because the inequality uses $<$ rather than $\le$.
Although 6 is outside the interval, it is not the endpoint being tested. The notation specifically includes 0 but excludes the upper boundary 5.

cards.front: Class width = [ ___ ].
cards.back: Class width = upper boundary - lower boundary.

options.explanation: Class width measures the distance from the lower boundary to the upper boundary, so it is calculated by subtracting the lower boundary from the upper boundary.
Reversing the subtraction produces a negative value for an ordinary class interval. Class width is found using upper boundary - lower boundary.
Adding the boundaries does not measure the size of the interval and may instead relate to finding twice its midpoint. Class width uses upper boundary - lower boundary.
Subtracting the midpoint from the upper boundary gives only half the class width for a standard interval. The full width is upper boundary - lower boundary.

cards.front: A histogram’s vertical axis shows [ ___ ] and its horizontal axis shows [ ___ ].
cards.back: A histogram’s vertical axis shows frequency density and its horizontal axis shows class intervals.

options.text: A histogram’s vertical axis shows frequency density and its horizontal axis shows class intervals.
options.explanation: Frequency density determines each bar’s height and is plotted vertically. The horizontal axis contains the continuous class intervals whose widths form the bases of the bars.

options.text: A histogram’s vertical axis shows frequency and its horizontal axis shows class intervals.
options.explanation: Frequency is represented by bar area, not generally by the vertical axis. The vertical axis shows frequency density, while the horizontal axis shows class intervals.

options.text: A histogram’s vertical axis shows frequency density and its horizontal axis shows frequency.
options.explanation: The horizontal axis represents the measured variable divided into class intervals, not frequency. Frequency density is vertical, and each bar’s area gives its frequency.

options.text: A histogram’s vertical axis shows class intervals and its horizontal axis shows frequency density.
options.explanation: This reverses the axes. Class intervals run along the horizontal axis, while frequency density is plotted on the vertical axis to determine bar height.

cards.front: Why do neighbouring histogram bars normally touch?

options.explanation: Continuous data can take any value throughout adjoining class intervals, so neighbouring histogram bars touch to show that there are no gaps between those ranges.
Discrete data consists of separate countable values and is commonly displayed with gaps between bars. Histogram bars normally touch because the underlying data is continuous.
Categorical groups are separate and are usually displayed using a bar chart with gaps. Histogram bars touch because they represent adjoining intervals of continuous data.
Whether values are ungrouped does not explain touching bars, and histograms use grouped intervals. The bars touch because the represented data is continuous.

cards.front: Find the class width of $4 \le t < 9$.

options.explanation: The class width is the upper boundary minus the lower boundary, so $9 - 4 = 5$.
This comes from adding the two boundaries, $9 + 4$, rather than finding the distance between them. The correct class width is $9 - 4 = 5$.
This uses the lower boundary itself instead of calculating the interval’s width. Subtracting the boundaries gives $9 - 4 = 5$.
This uses the upper boundary itself instead of measuring the distance between the boundaries. The class width is $9 - 4 = 5$.

cards.front: What formula gives frequency from class width and frequency density?

options.explanation: A histogram bar’s frequency is represented by its area. Multiplying the class width by the frequency density gives this area and therefore the class frequency.
Dividing frequency density by class width does not calculate the bar’s area. Frequency is found by multiplying class width by frequency density.
This incorrectly divides the class width by the bar height. Histogram frequency is the bar’s area, so class width must be multiplied by frequency density.
Adding the width and density confuses the dimensions of the histogram bar. Its frequency is represented by area, calculated as class width multiplied by frequency density.

cards.front: A bar covers 5 to 13 hours with frequency density 2.5. Find the frequency.

options.explanation: The class width is $13-5=8$ hours. Multiplying this by the frequency density gives the frequency: $8\times2.5=20$.
This comes from multiplying the lower boundary, 5, by 2.5 instead of using the class width. The width is $13-5=8$, giving frequency $20$.
This uses the upper boundary, 13, as the class width. The actual width is $13-5=8$, so the frequency is $8\times2.5=20$.
This divides the class width by the frequency density rather than finding the bar’s area. The correct calculation is $8\times2.5=20$.

cards.front: Why is height alone not the frequency when class widths are unequal?

options.explanation: In a histogram, frequency is represented by each bar’s area. Therefore both class width and frequency density, shown by height, determine the frequency.

options.text: Frequency is height: the frequency density alone.
options.explanation: Height represents frequency density, not frequency. When class widths differ, equal heights can produce different areas, so frequency must be calculated as width multiplied by height.

options.text: Frequency is width: upper boundary $-$ lower boundary.
options.explanation: The difference between the class boundaries gives only the class width. Frequency is represented by the whole bar area, calculated as width multiplied by height.
A bar’s perimeter has no statistical meaning in a histogram. Frequency is represented by area, so it is found by multiplying the class width by the height.

cards.front: What formula gives frequency density from frequency and class width?

options.explanation: Frequency equals class width multiplied by frequency density. Rearranging this relationship gives frequency density as frequency divided by class width.
This reverses the required division. Since frequency equals class width multiplied by frequency density, divide frequency by class width to obtain frequency density.
Multiplication is used to recover frequency from density and width, not to find density. Frequency density is frequency divided by class width.
Subtracting class width from frequency does not represent the histogram relationship. Frequency density is calculated by dividing the frequency by the class width.

cards.front: A class has frequency 24 and class width 6. Find the frequency density.

options.explanation: Frequency density is frequency divided by class width. Therefore the density is $24\div6=4$.
This multiplies $24$ by $6$, which would find frequency if 24 were a density. Here density is required, so calculate $24\div6=4$.
This reverses the division by calculating $6\div24$. Frequency density is frequency divided by class width, so the correct calculation is $24\div6=4$.
This subtracts the class width from the frequency, but frequency density is a quotient. Dividing $24$ by $6$ gives the correct density of $4$.

cards.front: Before choosing the vertical scale for a histogram, what value should you check?

options.explanation: Bar height represents frequency density, so the vertical axis must reach at least the greatest density. Checking this value allows a suitable scale to be selected.
The largest frequency may belong to a wide class and need not create the tallest bar. The vertical scale must accommodate the largest frequency density.
Class width controls horizontal bar width rather than vertical height. To choose the vertical scale, identify the largest frequency density.
Total frequency describes the whole data set and does not determine any individual bar’s height. The vertical scale should be based on the largest frequency density.

cards.front: A bar covers 15 to 20 with frequency density 3.6. Find the frequency.

options.explanation: The class width is $20-15=5$. Multiplying width by frequency density gives the frequency: $5\times3.6=18$.
This adds the width, 5, to the density, 3.6, instead of calculating the bar’s area. The correct calculation is $5\times3.6=18$.
This divides the density by the class width, reversing the histogram area calculation. Frequency is width multiplied by density, so $5\times3.6=18$.
This treats the upper boundary, 20, as the class width. The actual width is $20-15=5$, so the frequency is $5\times3.6=18$.

cards.front: Two bars have the same height. One class is twice as wide. How do the frequencies compare?
cards.back: The wider class has twice the frequency.

options.text: The wider class has twice the frequency.
options.explanation: Equal heights mean equal frequency densities. Since frequency is width multiplied by height, doubling the width while keeping the height fixed doubles the frequency.

options.text: The wider class has the same frequency.
options.explanation: Equal bar heights mean equal frequency densities, not equal frequencies. The wider bar has twice the area, so its class has twice the frequency.

options.text: The wider class has half the frequency.
options.explanation: This reverses the effect of increasing class width. With equal heights, doubling the width doubles the bar’s area and therefore doubles the frequency.

options.text: The wider class has four times the frequency.
options.explanation: This incorrectly treats frequency as if both dimensions had doubled. Only the width doubles while height stays fixed, so the area and frequency merely double.

cards.front: Missing frequency: interval 10 up to 18, frequency density 0.75.

options.explanation: Frequency equals class width multiplied by frequency density. The interval width is $18-10=8$, so the frequency is $8\times0.75=6$.
This comes from adding the class width and density rather than multiplying them. Frequency is area, so it is $(18-10)\times0.75=6$.
This uses the upper class boundary as the class width. The actual width is $18-10=8$, giving a frequency of $8\times0.75=6$.
This divides the class width by the frequency density. Histogram frequency is found by multiplying width by density, so $8\times0.75=6$.

cards.front: Missing frequency density: interval 18 up to 30, frequency 18.

options.explanation: Frequency density equals frequency divided by class width. The width is $30-18=12$, so the density is $18\div12=1.5$.
This reverses the required division by calculating class width divided by frequency. Density is frequency divided by width, so $18\div12=1.5$.
This incorrectly uses $18-12$ after finding the class width. Frequency density requires division: $18\div(30-18)=1.5$.
This uses the lower boundary as though it were the class width. The width is $30-18=12$, so the density is $18\div12=1.5$.

cards.front: A bar runs 20 to 35 minutes with frequency density 2. Estimate the frequency from 25 to 35 minutes.

options.explanation: The requested section has width $35-25=10$ minutes. Its estimated frequency is its histogram area, so $10\times2=20$.
This uses the full bar width of $35-20=15$ minutes. Only the section from 25 to 35 is required, giving $10\times2=20$.
This gives only the width of the requested section and ignores the frequency density. Multiplying by the density gives $10\times2=20$.
This reports the full class width rather than the frequency for the requested section. The relevant histogram area is $(35-25)\times2=20$.

cards.front: What assumption is made when estimating frequency within part of a class interval?
cards.back: The data is evenly spread within the class.

options.text: The data is evenly spread within the class.
options.explanation: A histogram does not show how values are distributed inside each class. Estimating a proportion of a class therefore assumes uniform distribution within that interval.

options.text: The data is concentrated at the midpoint within the class.
options.explanation: Equal concentration at the midpoint would not justify using widths to estimate proportions. The required assumption is that the data is evenly spread throughout the class.

options.text: The data is increasing steadily within the class.
options.explanation: A steadily increasing distribution would place more observations near the upper boundary and make area proportions invalid. The estimate assumes the data is evenly spread within the class.

options.text: The data is decreasing steadily within the class.
options.explanation: A steadily decreasing distribution would place more observations near the lower boundary. Proportional estimation instead relies on assuming that the data is evenly spread within the class.
